[b]some tips before buying/playing?[/b]
- the writing may stutter or be... [i]abstract[/i]... at times. the dialogue feels realistic considering the characters but it may be a put-off for some, especially because the lore is left mostly unexplained and the dialogue can seem trivial or inconsecuential, [b]but i assure you it's not[/b].
- [b]don't play wktd expecting a fully-fleshed pierced-together story with a narrative that will accompany you from beginning to end[/b]. it's told like a string of events that happen in the end of a summer camp and the relationship between 3 girls and their peers. you'll have to make assumptions for what isn't directly said, and your first playthrough may feel rushed since you still won't know much about the characters' struggles and stuff.
- [b]the ost is amazing for building the atmosphere[/b], be wary of sudden noises and radio static, play at low volume if needed.
- [b]the game is slightly short and pretty straightforward to 100%[/b], but if you relate to the message [b]it will stay with you[/b]. it's like seeing a tv glow.

Los protagonistas con nombres de planetas han sido enviados a un campamento de verano cristiano por ser, cada uno a su manera, “malos”. Este campamento casi parece uno de supervivencia, con el Diablo rondando y siendo responsabilidad de los niños pugnar a esta presencia maligna, con el frecuente aviso de las sirenas en forma de chirridos agudos y rasposos, como si alguien arañase unas pizarras que habitan dentro de nuestros oídos. Sin embargo, la verdadera naturaleza de esta entidad es una pieza clave para desvelar el significado de los conceptos de “maldad” y “bondad” en este corto videojuego y cómo estos se vinculan —o rehúyen— a Venus, Jupiter y Neptune, adolescentes vulnerables víctimas de un trauma religioso, incapaces de poder sentirse en armonía con sus propios cuerpos o de relacionarse sin dejarle un hueco al Diablo entre ellos sin querer. Personas catalogadas como defectuosas que tratan de ganarse un hueco en el Reino de los Cielos a pesar de su muy limitado aforo, gente desplazada de la calidez de sus hogares por un mal comportamiento que no puede ser corregido por métodos convencionales y que se oculta de puertas afuera como si nada ocurriese. “Aquí no ha pasado nada” es una frase que han escuchado mil veces. No son jóvenes con problemas que no van mucho más allá de amoríos de película que podrían solucionarse intercambiando un par de palabras, sino mártires de una dura realidad material de la que son demasiado jóvenes para defenderse por sí mismos. No provocan grima en mí, sino ternura y compasión.

Si Dios les rechaza por lo que son, ¿de verdad es tan malo aceptar a un Diablo amoroso dentro de sus corazones, uno capaz de acoger a las tres personas en su reino? Dios es lejano, pero al Diablo le conocemos muy bien.

We Know the Devil sabe representar muy bien la experiencia de ser un adolescente LGBT en conflicto consigo mismo y especialmente con su entorno, como si no fuera más que un defecto en el seno de una sociedad ultrarreligiosa que los mira con malos ojos. Si bien es cierto que su escritura está muy lejos de ser perfecta, me recuerda mucho a Umineko no Naku Koro ni en el sentido de que derrocha pasión y sinceridad, como si quien lo haya escrito hubiera tenido la repentina necesidad de arrancarse todas esas emociones del pecho, logrando plasmar la vulnerabilidad emocional que oprime a sus protagonistas en el muy sentido texto.

On my first playthrough of this game, I couldn't help but feel a bit… lost. The game keeps presenting you with choices comprising two characters whose immediate and long-term consequences are entirely unclear. Aside from those, it has very casual yet often cryptic dialogue full of Christian motifs (I'm agnostic) and rather frequent typos. The writer was clearly enjoying themselves communicating as those teenagers, but it makes it a bit challenging to discern intentional plot points from quirky humor. As a result, the (red) ending feels quite abrupt, and I couldn't entirely discern how my choices led to it. However, I was already really appreciating the game's artwork.

After looking up a completion guide, the reason for my first ending became more apparent, and I also started to enjoy the writing of the other routes quite a bit more. Exploring all the different dialogues that emerge as you make the choices and piecing together information about the characters actually became fun! The highlight of the rest of the game, however, was definitely the true ending: the game finally tells you what it is actually about while resolving everyone's conflict, and it's so much more explicit and beautiful than I had been hoping for.

While I absolutely think that the intransparency about the effects of your decisions is part of what defines this game, I can't exactly claim to have had fun in the beginning before looking up the guide and I think it may have been beneficial to follow the more traditional approach of having the story diverge before the ending. I understand that it's very much possible to 100% the game without one if you experiment enough, but I clearly didn't have the patience.
